title: The Call of Samuel
overview: 1 Samuel 3 narrates the divine calling of the young boy Samuel, marking a pivotal moment in Israel’s history. During a time when prophetic revelation was rare, God calls Samuel repeatedly at night, and through the guidance of Eli, Samuel learns to respond to God's voice. This chapter reveals the transition from the old priestly leadership of Eli’s house, marked by corruption and judgment, to the rise of Samuel as a faithful prophet. The chapter highlights God’s sovereign initiative in calling and commissioning His servants, the importance of obedience, and the seriousness of sin and judgment. It sets the stage for Samuel’s prophetic ministry and the eventual establishment of the monarchy in Israel.
structure:
**Verses 1-5: The Setting and First Calls.** The chapter opens by describing the spiritual climate—God’s word was rare—and introduces Samuel ministering under Eli. Samuel hears God calling but mistakes the voice for Eli’s.

**Verses 6-10: Samuel’s Third Call and Eli’s Instruction.** After two more calls, Eli realizes God is speaking to Samuel and instructs him how to respond, leading to Samuel’s obedient reply, "Speak; for thy servant heareth."

**Verses 11-14: The Divine Revelation of Judgment.** God reveals to Samuel the coming judgment on Eli’s house due to the iniquity of his sons and Eli’s failure to restrain them, emphasizing divine justice.

**Verses 15-18: Samuel’s Fear and Confession to Eli.** Samuel hesitates to share the vision but ultimately tells Eli everything, demonstrating transparency and submission to God’s will.

**Verses 19-21: Samuel’s Growth and Recognition.** The chapter closes by affirming Samuel’s growth, God’s presence with him, and his recognition as a prophet throughout Israel, with God revealing Himself again in Shiloh.

keyVerses.text: And the LORD came, and stood, and called as at other times, Samuel, Samuel. Then Samuel answered, Speak; for thy servant heareth.
keyVerses.significance: This verse marks Samuel’s obedient response to God’s call, symbolizing the beginning of his prophetic ministry and exemplifying the ideal attitude of a servant ready to listen to God.

keyVerses.text: And the LORD said to Samuel, Behold, I will do a thing in Israel, at which both the ears of every one that heareth it shall tingle.
keyVerses.significance: God’s declaration of impending judgment introduces a major theme of divine justice and signals a significant turning point in Israel’s history, emphasizing the seriousness of God’s word.

keyVerses.text: And therefore I have sworn unto the house of Eli, that the iniquity of Eli's house shall not be purged with sacrifice nor offering for ever.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals the irrevocable judgment on Eli’s family due to persistent sin, underscoring the holiness of God and the consequences of failing to uphold His standards.

keyVerses.text: And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him, and did let none of his words fall to the ground.
keyVerses.significance: This verse affirms God’s presence with Samuel and the effectiveness of his prophetic ministry, highlighting God’s faithfulness in raising up leaders who faithfully communicate His word.

characters.name: Samuel
characters.description: A young boy serving under Eli who receives his first prophetic call from God. Samuel’s obedience and willingness to listen mark the beginning of his significant role as a prophet and judge in Israel.

characters.name: Eli
characters.description: The high priest and mentor to Samuel, whose failing eyesight and spiritual decline contrast with Samuel’s rising prophetic role. Eli recognizes God’s call to Samuel and instructs him on how to respond.

characters.name: The LORD
characters.description: God actively calls Samuel to serve as His prophet, revealing His plans for judgment on Eli’s house and demonstrating His sovereign control over Israel’s spiritual leadership.

themes.description: The chapter centers on God’s initiative in calling Samuel, illustrating how God chooses and equips servants to fulfill His purposes, a theme echoed throughout Scripture in the lives of prophets and leaders.
Samuel’s response, "Speak; for thy servant heareth," models the believer’s attitude toward God’s word—ready and obedient—highlighting the importance of hearing and responding to God’s voice.
God’s judgment on Eli’s house for sin and neglect underscores the holiness of God and the serious consequences of disobedience, reinforcing the biblical principle that sin cannot be ignored.
The chapter marks a transition from Eli’s flawed priestly leadership to Samuel’s prophetic ministry, symbolizing God’s faithfulness in raising new leaders to guide His people.

historicalContext: This chapter is set during the period of the Judges, a time characterized by social and spiritual instability in Israel before the establishment of the monarchy. Shiloh, where the tabernacle and the ark of the covenant were located, was the religious center. The priesthood was hereditary, with Eli serving as high priest, but his sons’ corrupt behavior had led to a decline in spiritual leadership. The political situation was fragmented, with Israel lacking centralized governance, and prophetic voices were rare, making Samuel’s call especially significant. The cultural context includes the importance of hearing God’s voice through priests and prophets, and the expectation of obedience to God’s covenant.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This perspective emphasizes God’s sovereign election in calling Samuel and the necessity of spiritual awakening through God’s initiative. Samuel’s obedience is seen as a model for believers responding to God’s call, and Eli’s judgment highlights the consequences of failing to uphold covenant faithfulness.

Dispensationalists highlight the distinct roles of priest and prophet, viewing Samuel’s call as a transition to prophetic leadership preparing for the coming monarchy. The judgment on Eli’s house is understood within the framework of God’s unfolding plan for Israel’s governance.

Early church interpreters often saw Samuel as a type of Christ, a faithful servant called by God to speak His word. Eli’s blindness is interpreted spiritually as a symbol of failing to perceive God’s will, while Samuel’s hearing represents spiritual receptivity.

crossReferences.connection: Like Samuel, Jeremiah receives a direct call from God at a young age, emphasizing God’s sovereign choice and commissioning of prophets.
Isaiah’s response, "Here am I; send me," parallels Samuel’s readiness to hear and obey God’s call.
Jesus teaches that His sheep hear His voice, reflecting the theme of listening to God’s call as demonstrated by Samuel.
Samuel is listed among the heroes of faith who obeyed God’s call, highlighting his role in the biblical narrative of faithfulness.
The psalmist’s desire to hear what God will speak echoes Samuel’s attentive listening to God’s voice.

application: Be attentive and ready to hear God’s voice in daily life, responding with obedience like Samuel.
Recognize the importance of spiritual mentorship and guidance, as Eli provided for Samuel.
Understand that God’s word is powerful and effective; commit to faithfully proclaiming and living it.
Acknowledge the seriousness of sin and its consequences, striving for holiness in personal and communal life.
Trust God’s sovereign plan even when His ways involve judgment or difficult transitions.
Cultivate a heart posture that says, "Speak, Lord; for thy servant heareth," in prayer and study.
conclusion: 1 Samuel 3 stands as a foundational chapter illustrating God’s sovereign call and the birth of prophetic ministry in Israel. It teaches believers the vital importance of listening for God’s voice with humility and obedience, while also warning of the consequences of spiritual failure. Samuel’s faithful response and God’s presence with him encourage Christians to trust in God’s guidance and to be faithful witnesses of His word. The chapter’s themes of divine calling, judgment, and leadership transition continue to resonate, reminding believers that God actively works through His servants to fulfill His redemptive purposes.
timeline: c. 1100 BC - Period of the Judges, prior to Israel’s monarchy

outline.heading: Samuel’s Initial Call and Mistaken Response
outline.description: Samuel, serving under Eli, hears God calling but mistakes the voice for Eli’s, illustrating the beginning of his spiritual awakening.

outline.heading: Eli’s Instruction and Samuel’s Obedient Reply
outline.description: After multiple calls, Eli instructs Samuel how to respond, leading to Samuel’s first clear communication with God, marking his prophetic commissioning.

outline.heading: God’s Revelation of Judgment on Eli’s House
outline.description: God reveals His judgment against Eli’s family due to their sin, highlighting divine justice and the consequences of failing to uphold holiness.

outline.heading: Samuel’s Fear and Confession to Eli
outline.description: Samuel hesitates but ultimately shares God’s message with Eli, demonstrating transparency and submission to God’s will.

outline.heading: Samuel’s Growth and Recognition as Prophet
outline.description: The chapter concludes with Samuel’s spiritual growth, God’s presence with him, and his recognition throughout Israel as a true prophet.
